tldr: The paper introduces Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE), a variance reduction scheme for policy gradients that balances bias and variance via parameters γ and λ, combined with trust region optimization for both policy and value function neural networks, enabling effective high-dimensional continuous control.
contributions: Novel analysis and justification for generalized advantage estimation (GAE), applicable in both online and batch settings, building on prior work by Kimura & Kobayashi (1998) and Wawrzyński (2009)
Proposal of trust region optimization for value function training, described as a robust and efficient way to train neural network value functions with thousands of parameters

An algorithm combining GAE and trust region methods that empirically learns neural network policies for challenging 3D locomotion tasks, extending the state of the art in reinforcement learning for high-dimensional continuous control
methods: The authors propose GAE(γ,λ), an exponentially-weighted estimator of the advantage function defined as the discounted sum of TD residuals: Â_GAE = Σ(γλ)^l δ_V_{t+l}. The parameter γ acts as a variance reduction factor (introducing bias when <1), while λ controls the bias-variance tradeoff in the advantage estimate. Both policy and value functions are represented by neural networks with over 10^4 parameters each. Policy optimization uses trust region policy optimization (TRPO) with KL divergence constraints, and value function optimization uses a trust region method solved via conjugate gradients with a Gauss-Newton Hessian approximation.
results: The algorithm learned complex running gaits for bipedal and quadrupedal simulated robots in 3D locomotion tasks, and learned a policy for getting a biped to stand up from lying on the ground. Policies perform torque-level control of simulated 3D robots with up to 33 state dimensions and 10 actuators. The amount of simulated experience required for 3D biped tasks corresponds to 1-2 weeks of real time. Unlike prior work using hand-crafted policy representations, their neural network policies map directly from raw kinematics to joint torques. The approach is fully model-free.
limitations: Using γ < 1 introduces bias into the policy gradient estimate regardless of value function accuracy. Using λ < 1 introduces bias when the value function is inaccurate. The approach requires 1-2 weeks of real simulated time for learning on 3D bipeds. The experiments are conducted in simulation only, with no mention of real-world robot deployment.
